cells.tense: You are handing something on right now, and you know what you're doing with it.
cells.ask: Give someone the version of what you carry that fits their life, not yours, and see whether it lands.
cells.core:
What you pass along arrives shaped for the person receiving it. Not repeated word for word because that's how it came to you, and not trimmed until it fits just any listener. You've found the difference between keeping something alive and keeping it unchanged, and you're working on the right side of that.

The small adjustments are the actual work — knowing when to give the whole thing and when to give just enough, when to say it your way and when to say it theirs. Tuning like that doesn't finish. Each person you hand it to asks something a little different of you, and answering that is what keeps it worth having. You've already got the feel for it.
cells.sheetLine: You pass things on shaped for the person receiving them.
cells.verb: To pass on what's worth carrying

cells.tense: You're bracing to make sure they get it right, and steeling yourself for them not to.
cells.ask: Let one thing you'd normally correct stand exactly as someone else said it, and keep your hands off it for a day.
cells.core:
You hold the shape of this so tightly that gripping has become the point. Out in front of you is a picture where the people close to you finally get it — agree, repeat it correctly, stop drifting from what you know is true — and you're already living in that picture, correcting toward it. The correcting has crowded out the closeness it was supposed to protect.

What you're protecting is worth protecting. But when the exact form matters more than the person in front of you, the form stops being something anyone wants to receive. Something built on a false premise gives way when the truth shows up, and you don't get to pick what falls or when. What's yours to do is loosen the grip enough that something new can still reach you.

cells.tense: You left that behind a long while ago, and you're still standing in its doorway.
cells.ask: Sit with one person and tell them something you actually do, not something you think — no lesson on top of it.
cells.core:
Nothing behind you is coming forward with you, so each new person you meet starts from zero. You know plenty. But none of it feels like it belongs to anything bigger, so nothing adds up and nothing gets handed along. Company isn't the absent part. The absent part is a frame two people could stand inside together and call ours.

Charging that back up doesn't happen by pushing harder at the connection itself. It happens by seeing the pattern underneath, the thing that makes two separate experiences recognizably alike. Once that becomes visible, the connection keeps itself. Until then the space stays empty no matter who's in it.

cells.tense: You are already the one people learn from, and you are calling it something else.
cells.ask: Say out loud that one thing you do in your own way is yours, not just how it's done.
cells.core:
People around you are picking things up — how you talk, what you bother with, the way you handle a situation — and they're taking it with them. You'd call it nothing special, just what you do. The passing-on is running anyway. The only part not in place is you knowing it's yours.

What you call ordinary is a way of doing things that other people are adopting because it works. That's not a small thing. Name one piece of it as yours, at whatever scale feels true. Not a claim to own it — just an acknowledgment that you're the one carrying it. The adjusting after that takes care of itself.

attempts.check: The claim the record doesn't support is anything about who taught them this or when the pattern started. A reader could reasonably say the stakes aren't this high, that they're just carrying on how things are done. If my read is wrong, the act of passing something on with attention given to who receives it is still useful because it's about how they transmit, not what they carry. The sentence that serves me more than them would be anything that makes their way of carrying things sound like the problem itself.
